title: Fixup and Autosquash
description: Use git commit --fixup and git rebase --autosquash to automatically apply corrections without manual todo list editing.

data.text: The --fixup flag to git commit creates a commit whose message references an earlier commit. When you pair it with git rebase --autosquash, Git automatically finds the right place for the fixup and squashes it — no manual todo list editing required.

git commit --fixup <commit> creates a new commit with a message of the form fixup! <original-message>. Git uses the original message's hash to identify the target commit, so even if the message changes slightly, the fixup is matched correctly.

data.title: Create fixup and squash commits
data.code:
# Create a fixup commit for the 2nd-to-last commit
git commit --fixup HEAD~2

# Create a squash commit for the last commit
git commit --squash HEAD~1

# Verify the commit messages were created correctly
git log --oneline -3

data.text: When you pass --autosquash to git rebase -i, Git scans the todo list for fixup and squash commits, moves them directly after their target commit, and marks them with the correct action. The resulting todo list is fully prepared — you just save and close.

data.title: Rebase with --autosquash
data.code:
# Step 1: Make some changes
git add -p
git commit --fixup HEAD~3

# Step 2: Run rebase with --autosquash
git rebase -i --autosquash HEAD~4

# Step 3: Git opens editor with todo list already prepared
# Step 4: Save and close — done!

data.title: Configure autosquash as the default
data.text: Run git config --global rebase.autoSquash true to make --autosquash the default behavior for all interactive rebases. This eliminates a flag from your workflow without any downside.
When to use fixup vs squash commits

items: **fixup** — For corrections, typo fixes, and missed edge cases. The message is discarded.
**squash** — For commits whose messages should be merged into the target message.
**Manual squash** — When the fixup/squash is not a clean 1:1 mapping.

data.text: A common pattern is to commit frequently during feature development, then use fixup for small corrections discovered during review. This keeps the main feature commit clean while preserving all the detail in the Git object history (in case you need to investigate later).

data.title: Review-driven fixup workflow
data.code:
# After a PR review identifies issues:
# Fix issue #1 — add validation
# Fix issue #2 — update error message

# Each fix gets its own fixup commit
git add -p src/auth/LoginService.cs
git commit --fixup HEAD~4

git add -p src/auth/LoginService.cs
git commit --fixup HEAD~3

# Rebase with --autosquash
git rebase -i --autosquash HEAD~6

# Force push with lease
git push --force-with-lease origin feature/auth

items.question: Can I have multiple fixup commits for the same target?
items.answer: Yes. Each fixup commit is applied in order. Git processes them sequentially during the rebase.

items.question: Will --autosquash work across non-consecutive commits?
items.answer: Yes. Git identifies the target commit by its SHA-1 hash embedded in the fixup message, not by position.

items.question: What if the target commit no longer exists?
items.answer: The rebase will fail because the fixup commit cannot find its target. Use git rebase --abort to cancel and either recreate the fixup or squash manually.

items.question: Can I amend a fixup commit?
items.answer: Yes. Edit the fixup commit with git rebase -i and change fixup to edit, then amend as needed during the rebase.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: --fixup creates a commit targeting a specific earlier commit
--autosquash automates placing and squashing fixup commits
Configure rebase.autoSquash to make --autosquash the default
fixup discards the secondary message; squash merges it
Use fixup for review-driven corrections during feature development
